power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Kidney stones are a disorder in which urinary solutes precipitate to form crystalline aggregates in the urinary space.
The blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio (BAR), a nutrition and inflammatory indicator, has an unclear association with kidney stones.

Methods: Using NHANES 2007-2020 data, we compared baseline characteristics between kidney stone formers and controls and evaluated the BAR-stone relationship via weighted multivariate logistic regression (WMLR), restricted cubic splines (RCS), stratification analyses, and XGBoost, and performed an exploratory analysis in an ICU cohort, the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV).
Results: A total of 23,652 participants (2,318 with kidney stones) were included, and 21 baseline features differed significantly between groups (P < 0.05).

text.text: Four progressively adjusted models were constructed.
Model 1 (unadjusted model) included only BAR as the independent variable.
Model 2 (partially adjusted model) additionally adjusted for age, sex, and race/ethnicity.

Model 3 (conventionally adjusted model) further adjusted for marital status, education level, smoking status, alcohol consumption, dietary intake, and a series of chronic disease histories and laboratory parameters, i.e., the adjustment set used in previous analyses of BAR and kidney stones.
Model 4 (fully adjusted, primary model) additionally adjusted for BMI, diabetes, eGFR and PIR.

These four variables were included a priori because BUN and albumin are both strongly determined by glomerular filtration and nutritional status, so that a BAR-stone association observed without them cannot be attributed to BAR itself.
Model 3 is reported alongside Model 4 to show how the estimate changes once renal function and metabolic status are accounted for, and to allow direct comparison with earlier studies.
All models specified a binomial distribution with a logit link function, and hypothesis tests for regression coefficients were based on Wald tests with robust standard errors.
Results are presented as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

text.text: To characterize the dose-response relationship between kidney stones and BAR, restricted cubic splines (RCS) with four knots placed at the 5th, 35th, 65th and 95th percentiles of BAR were fitted within the survey-weighted design, and departure from linearity was assessed by a Wald test of the nonlinear spline terms.
RCS models were fitted without adjustment and with adjustment for the Model 3 covariates.
When nonlinearity was detected, segmented regression was used to estimate the inflection point, i.e., the BAR value at which the slope of the dose-response curve changes.
Because a change in slope of a fitted spline does not by itself establish a biological threshold, the inflection point was interpreted descriptively.
To further explore the stability of the correlation between kidney stones and BAR in different subgroups, we employed stratification analysis to replay Model 3 in each subgroup.

Age was categorized as < 50 or ≥ 50 years, BMI as < 25 or ≥ 25 kg/m², PIR as < 1.3 or ≥ 1.3 (the federal poverty threshold), eGFR as < 60 or ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m², and dietary intakes were dichotomized at their medians.

text.text: Its components, BUN and albumin, are intrinsically linked to kidney physiology [8, 13]; elevated BUN has been associated with hematuria in patients with kidney stones, and albumin is negatively correlated with kidney stone prevalence after multivariate adjustment [10].

text.text: These observations motivated the present analysis, in which kidney stone formers had higher BAR levels and also differed from controls in several conventional risk factors.

Weighted multivariable logistic regression showed a positive association in the unadjusted model and after adjustment for a broad set of demographic, lifestyle, dietary, comorbidity and laboratory variables (Model 3), but the association was attenuated to the null once BMI, diabetes, eGFR and PIR were added (Model 4).
The apparent nonlinear relationship, and the inflection point at approximately 5.4 seen in the unadjusted analysis, were likewise not retained after adjustment.

Taken together, these results suggest that the crude association between BAR and kidney stones largely reflects confounding by renal function and metabolic status, rather than an independent effect of BAR.

text.text: Furthermore, an elevated risk of cardiovascular diseases-such as stroke, hypertension, and CHD-has been observed in patients with kidney stones.
This association may involve mechanisms such as vascular calcification, osteopontininduced oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction [28, 29].

In our data, the association did not differ materially across subgroups defined by sex, smoking status, cardiovascular disease or age (all P for interaction > 0.05), and adjusting for these variables in Model 3 did not attenuate the estimate; the attenuation appeared only when renal function and metabolic status were accounted for.

text.text: The attenuation observed after adjustment for eGFR is biologically plausible.
BAR is the ratio of BUN to albumin, and both analytes are strongly determined by glomerular filtration and by the patient's nutritional and inflammatory state [6, 7].
text.formatted: BAR is the ratio of BUN to albumin, and both analytes are strongly determined by glomerular filtration and by the patient's nutritional and inflammatory state <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: BUN rises with reduced renal perfusion and impaired filtration, so BAR partly encodes renal function; eGFR is therefore not a neutral covariate but one that shares a common cause 25 with the exposure.

When eGFR, BMI and diabetes were added, the BAR estimate moved towards unity, which is the pattern expected when an observed association is confounded by these factors rather than generated by the exposure itself.
The incremental models showed that BMI, diabetes and eGFR each contributed to this attenuation, whereas PIR did not.

BAR therefore retains descriptive value as an index that combines nutritional and inflammatory information, but our data do not support its use as an independent risk marker for stones once renal function and metabolic status are known.
Younger individuals represent a growing at-risk population for kidney disease, a trend driven in part by dietary shifts.
This age group also carries a substantial burden of hereditary kidney stones, which often present at a mean age of 30 ± 14 years [15], further underscoring the early onset of stone-related pathology.

text.text: In addition to genetic predisposition, younger populations exhibit a higher prevalence of nutritional risk and elevated blood urea nitrogen-to-creatinine ratios despite lower rates of normal nutritional status [30].

text.text: Moreover, adolescents and young adults show heightened susceptibility to the renal effects of long-term inorganic pollutant exposure, which has been correlated with BUN and albumin-to-creatinine ratios [31].

text.text: Collectively, these findings suggest that multiple pathways-dietary, genetic, nutritional, and environmental-converge to elevate kidney stone risk in young populations.
Previous analyses have suggested that indices combining BUN with nutritional markers may be particularly informative in young, malnourished populations [32].

text.text: In our data, however, 26 the BAR-stone estimate did not differ between participants younger and older than 50 years (P for interaction = 0.73; OR 1.07 in both groups), so we found no evidence of age-specific usefulness.
The rising burden of stone disease in this group is better addressed through the dietary and metabolic pathways described above.

Although the point estimate was higher in females than in males, the interaction test was not significant (P = 0.38), and the difference is more plausibly explained by differences in case numbers and precision than by a true sex-specific effect.
The same caution applies to the other subgroups in which the estimate happened to reach significance.

Previous reports linking BAR to mortality after surgery in critically ill patients [33] concerned a different outcome and a different population, and our data do not provide support for effect modification by sex in the stone setting.

text.text: Although inadequate hydration is a classic risk factor, the type of beverage consumed modulates this effect: magnesium-rich water may reduce stone risk, whereas hard water with high calcium content has been associated with increased risk in women over 60 [34].

text.text: In our 27 data the point estimate was higher in participants with high water intake (OR = 1.10, 95% CI 1.04-1.17) than in those with low intake (OR = 1.01, 95% CI 0.95-1.07), but the interaction term did not reach significance (P = 0.055), so this pattern should be regarded as hypothesis-generating.
Attention to water quality, with preference given to soft water or beverages with higher magnesium content, remains reasonable advice.
However, several limitations should be noted.
First, the cross-sectional nature of the NHANES dataset prevents causal inferences regarding the relationship between BAR and kidney stones, and reverse causation cannot be excluded.

Second, the use of self-reported data for stone history and for several other variables may have introduced recall and misclassification bias, and stone episodes are likely to have been under-ascertained.
Third, BAR was derived from a single measurement of BUN and albumin and therefore carries within-person variability.

Fourth, although eGFR was included as a covariate, a single creatinine-based estimate cannot fully capture renal tubular function or the prerenal components of BUN, so residual confounding by renal function remains possible; conversely, because BUN is itself a filtration marker, adjustment for eGFR may partly adjust away the exposure of interest, and the null estimate in Model 4 should be interpreted with this in mind.

Fifth, the exploratory MIMIC-IV analysis was based on administrative diagnosis codes, included few stone cases, and was not designed as external validation, so it can only indicate the direction of an association.

text.text: In this large, nationally representative sample of US adults, higher BAR was associated with kidney stones in models that did not account for renal function and metabolic status, but the association did not persist after adjustment for BMI, diabetes, eGFR and PIR, and no nonlinear threshold was retained after adjustment.
BAR should therefore be regarded as a marker that aggregates renal and metabolic risk rather than as an independent risk factor for kidney stones.
It does not appear to add information beyond established metabolic and renal measures, and it should not be used as a standalone risk marker.
Personalized precision prevention strategies for kidney stones should focus on the modifiable metabolic factors identified here, including obesity and diabetes, rather than on BAR itself.
